ACTIONS SECRETS: INHERIT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does secrets: inherit hand your secrets to the wrong workflow?

secrets: inherit on a reusable-workflow call passes every secret your workflow can see to the called workflow — not just the ones it needs. That is fine when the called workflow lives in the same repository you already review. It is a much bigger bet when it lives in another repository, or when the job that inherits it can be triggered by a stranger's fork. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds both patterns, each with the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeDetailFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added finding before it merges.

Common questions

What does secrets: inherit actually do?

On a reusable-workflow call (uses: OWNER/REPO/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref), secrets: inherit passes every secret the calling workflow can see to the called workflow — not just the ones it needs. GitHub's own documentation flags this as something to use with caution, especially when you do not control the called repository.

Why does it matter if the reusable workflow is in another repository?

A local reusable workflow (uses: ./.github/workflows/file.yml) lives in the same repository and the same review process as everything else. An external one (uses: OWNER/REPO/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref) is code you do not review on the same schedule — a compromised account, a force-pushed branch, or simply a maintainer decision at that other repository becomes a way to walk off with every secret you inherited to it.

Why does the trigger matter?

pull_request_target and workflow_run jobs run with the base repository's context even though a stranger's fork raised the event. secrets: inherit on such a job hands the fork-reachable run every secret the workflow can see, rather than the handful a job like "comment on the PR" actually needs.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste your workflow YAML and the scan runs entirely in this page.

Does a clean scan mean my workflows are safe?

No. This checks two specific, well-documented patterns in a single workflow file at a time. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your repository's overall security. It does not evaluate whether the called workflow is actually trustworthy, and it does not follow a local reusable workflow to see what it in turn calls.

More: what is secrets: inherit and when is it risky? · already run zizmor? see what its secrets-inherit audit does and does not check · reviewing workflows by hand instead? see where that holds up and where it slips.

← GitHub Actions secrets: inherit Check

GitHub Actions secrets: inherit Check vs. reviewing workflows by eye

Finding the line secrets: inherit in a workflow file takes no special skill. Deciding what it actually exposes -- whether the call it sits on reaches outside the repository, and whether the job is one a stranger's fork can trigger -- is the part that is easy to get wrong under a quick read. This page names no product or company; "reviewing by eye" is the generic habit every maintainer already has, not a competing tool.

Where a careful read holds up, and where it slips

secrets: inherit does not hide -- it is one line, and a reviewer who knows to look for it will find every instance in a file. What is harder to hold in your head while scanning a real workflow is what each instance actually means. A reusable-workflow call is external only if its uses: value names another repository (owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref) rather than a local path (./.github/workflows/file.yml) -- easy to conflate when the line wraps or sits several jobs away from the secrets: inherit it governs. And the fork-reachability question depends on a trigger declared once at the top of the file, under on:, which has to be carried in mind while reading down through every job below it -- easy to lose track of in a workflow with several unrelated jobs, especially when the risky job's name gives no hint that it is the one at risk.

Where to answer each question.
CaseReviewing by eyeThis tool
Spotting that a job uses secrets: inherit at allEasy to catch -- one distinctive lineCatches it the same way
Telling a local reusable-workflow call (./.github/workflows/file.yml) from an external one (owner/repo/…@ref)Easy to misread when the line wraps or sits jobs away from the secrets: inherit lineRe-parses the exact uses: value for every secrets: inherit line found
Connecting a job to a pull_request_target/workflow_run trigger declared at the top of a long fileEasy to lose track of while reading down through unrelated jobsChecks the whole file's trigger against every secrets: inherit line, however far apart they sit
A repository with a dozen workflow files, each with its own reusable-workflow callsRe-reading all of them for both patterns, every time a workflow changes, is tedious and easy to shortcutPaste as many files as you have, or run check.py across the whole directory
Blocking a newly-added finding before it mergesDepends on a human noticing it in reviewcheck.py --fail-on-risk gives a real exit code from the same classification, wired into your own CI

The two are complementary, not competing: this tool does not decide whether a called workflow is actually trustworthy, or whether a fork-reachable job's blast radius matters in your specific setup -- it replaces the tedious, error-prone part, which is re-checking every uses: value and every trigger declaration each time a workflow file changes.

Run the free secrets: inherit check

Common questions

What does reviewing a workflow for secrets: inherit by eye actually catch?

secrets: inherit is one distinctive line, and a reviewer who knows to look for it will find every occurrence in a file without much effort. That recognition is real, and this tool starts from the same line -- it does not find a secrets: inherit call a careful reader would have missed.

Why is telling an external reusable-workflow call from a local one easy to get wrong at a glance?

The difference between uses: ./.github/workflows/build.yml and uses: some-org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/build.yml@v2 is a leading ./ and an owner/repo prefix -- easy to miss when the uses: line is long, wrapped, or several jobs removed from the secrets: inherit line it governs. A reviewer scanning quickly for the string secrets: inherit can confirm the line exists without re-checking which uses: value the surrounding job actually calls, which is exactly the distinction that decides whether the finding is secrets-inherit-external-workflow at all. This tool re-reads the uses: value for every secrets: inherit line it finds, every time.

Why is the fork-trigger connection easy to miss even when the trigger is declared right there in the file?

pull_request_target and workflow_run are usually declared once, at the top of the file, under on:. The job carrying secrets: inherit can be dozens of lines below, in a workflow with several unrelated jobs. Holding "this file's trigger is untrusted" in mind while scanning down through every job's steps, for every workflow file in a repository, is the kind of bookkeeping that is easy to let slip -- especially on a workflow whose name or first job gives no hint that a later job is the one at risk. This tool checks the whole file's trigger against every secrets: inherit line it finds, regardless of how far apart they sit.

Does a clean result from this tool mean my repository's secret handling is safe?

No. It checks two specific, well-documented secrets: inherit patterns in one workflow file at a time. It does not evaluate whether a called reusable workflow is itself trustworthy, and it does not follow a local reusable workflow to see what it in turn calls -- both real ways a repository's secret handling can still be exposed after a clean scan.

vs-zizmor.html.text:
← GitHub Actions secrets: inherit Check

GitHub Actions secrets: inherit Check vs. zizmor

zizmor's secrets-inherit audit already flags secrets: inherit on a reusable-workflow call, local or external. This tool's matching finding covers the same external-workflow ground. What it adds is the one question that audit does not ask: is the job reachable from a stranger's fork in the first place?

What each tool is for

zizmor (github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis tool for GitHub Actions, installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor and run against workflow files or a whole repository. Its secrets-inherit audit, per its own documentation, detects excessive secret inheritance between a calling workflow and a reusable (called) workflow: any job whose uses: calls a reusable workflow with secrets: inherit, whether that workflow is local (./.github/workflows/file.yml) or external (owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref), on the reasoning that secrets: inherit violates the principle of least authority and makes it impossible to tell which exact secrets a reusable workflow actually ran with.

This checker makes the narrower secrets-inherit-external-workflow finding on the same external-repository pattern zizmor already covers -- and covers less of it, since it does not flag a local reusable-workflow call the way zizmor does. What it adds is secrets-inherit-untrusted-trigger: secrets: inherit on a job whose workflow is triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run, where a fork's pull request controls the event and the job still runs with the base repository's context. Per zizmor's published documentation and source, its secrets-inherit audit does not check which trigger a job runs on or whether a fork can reach it -- it flags the inheritance on its own, regardless of reachability.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to know whether any job in my repo hands a reusable workflow every secret with secrets: inherit, local or external.zizmor's secrets-inherit audit -- it covers both, this tool only the external half.
I want to know whether a pull_request_target or workflow_run job -- one a fork can trigger -- is the one holding secrets: inherit.This checker -- zizmor's audit does not check the trigger or fork-reachability at all.
I want one maintained scanner covering dozens of GitHub Actions security patterns beyond secret inheritance -- permissions, injection, cache poisoning, impostor commits, and more.zizmor -- that breadth is its whole job; this tool checks only the two secrets: inherit patterns above.
I don't want to install a CLI (pip or cargo) just to check one file.This checker -- it is a page, not a package. It only makes sense as a substitute for the external-workflow finding, though; for the trigger-reachability finding there is nothing else to substitute for.

Run zizmor for full coverage of the inheritance pattern, including local reusable workflows. This tool is worth a separate pass specifically for the trigger question -- a repository can pass zizmor's secrets-inherit audit today and still have a pull_request_target or workflow_run job handing a fork-reachable run every secret it can see, and nothing in that audit's stated scope would flag it.

Common questions

Does zizmor already catch secrets: inherit?

Yes, for the pattern itself. zizmor is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis CLI (installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor) whose secrets-inherit audit, per its own documentation, detects excessive secret inheritance between a calling workflow and a reusable (called) workflow -- any job whose uses: calls a reusable workflow with secrets: inherit, local (./.github/workflows/file.yml) or external (owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref) alike, on the reasoning that secrets: inherit violates the principle of least authority and makes it impossible to tell which exact secrets a reusable workflow ran with. This checker's secrets-inherit-external-workflow finding is the external-repository slice of that same pattern.

What does zizmor's secrets-inherit audit not check?

Per its published documentation and source, zizmor's secrets-inherit audit does not check whether the job carrying secrets: inherit is reachable from a pull_request_target or workflow_run trigger -- it flags the inheritance itself, regardless of which trigger runs the job or whether a fork can raise it. This checker's second finding, secrets-inherit-untrusted-trigger, is exactly that reachability check: secrets: inherit on a job whose workflow is triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run, where a stranger's fork controls the event.

So is this checker just a narrower copy of zizmor?

For one of its two findings, yes -- secrets-inherit-external-workflow covers ground zizmor's secrets-inherit audit already covers, and covers more broadly (zizmor also flags a local reusable-workflow call, which this tool does not, since a local call carries no different-repository risk). This tool's reason to exist is the other finding: secrets-inherit-untrusted-trigger, the pull_request_target/workflow_run reachability check that is outside the stated scope of zizmor's audit. If you already run zizmor, this tool adds that one check; it does not replace zizmor.

Why use a narrower tool instead of just running zizmor?

Two reasons, and only one is about coverage. First, zizmor is a CLI you install and point at files or a repository; this tool is a page you paste one file into, with nothing to install, which is faster for a single workflow you already have open. Second, and the one that matters: the untrusted-trigger finding is not in zizmor's secrets-inherit audit at all, so a clean zizmor scan can still carry a fork-reachable secrets: inherit call that only this tool's second finding names.

Does this tool need a GitHub token the way zizmor sometimes does?

No, never. zizmor documents an optional online mode -- set GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN -- for audits that benefit from GitHub API access. This tool has no online mode to opt into: nothing here talks to a server under any configuration, so there is no token to supply.

what-is-github-actions-secrets-inherit.h.text:
← Actions secrets: inherit Check

What is GitHub Actions secrets: inherit, and when is it risky?

A reusable workflow is a job that calls another workflow file instead of running its own steps directly:

jobs:
  call-workflow:
    uses: octo-org/example-repo/.github/workflows/reusable.yml@main
    secrets: inherit

secrets: inherit is a shorthand on a reusable-workflow call that passes every secret the calling workflow can see to the called workflow, instead of naming specific ones. It is risky in two independent ways: when the called workflow is hosted in a different repository you do not review on the same schedule, and when the job that inherits the secrets is reachable from a pull_request_target or workflow_run trigger a stranger's fork can raise.

By default, a reusable-workflow call receives no secrets at all — the caller has to name each one explicitly (secrets: { TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} }). That is convenient to skip, and GitHub's own documentation is upfront that skipping it should be used with caution.

Risk one: the called workflow is external

A reusable workflow can live in the same repository (uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable.yml) or in a different one entirely (uses: OWNER/REPO/.github/workflows/reusable.yml@ref). A local call is reviewed under the same process as everything else in your repository. An external call is code someone else controls — a compromised maintainer account, a force-pushed branch, or simply a decision made at that other repository becomes a way to walk off with every secret you inherited to it, not just the ones the workflow was written to use.

Risk two: the job is reachable from a fork

pull_request_target and workflow_run jobs run in the context of the base repository — with its secrets — even though the event that triggered them was raised by a stranger's fork. A job like "post a comment on the PR" might genuinely need one secret. secrets: inherit hands it the entire set, so a fork-reachable run has access to far more than the task in front of it requires.

Both risks are independent: a call can be external, fork-reachable, both, or neither.

The fix

  • Name the specific secrets a reusable workflow needs instead of inheriting all of them: secrets: { TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} }.
  • If you must inherit, pin the external call to a full commit SHA rather than a mutable branch or tag, so the code receiving your secrets cannot change without you updating the pin.
  • Keep a fork-reachable job (pull_request_target/workflow_run) on the smallest secret set it actually needs, or move the part that needs no secrets to the unprivileged pull_request trigger instead.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions secrets: inherit Check to find every external-workflow and fork-reachable secrets: inherit call across every workflow file at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any workflow has either pattern — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added one before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean a workflow is safe — only that these two documented patterns were not found.
